description:
ZXC team is exploring a question: where on Earth could we test technologies built for the Moon and Mars?

Based in Bishkek, we're interested in using satellite data, terrain analysis, and interactive mapping to investigate possible analog sites, including locations in Central Asia.

Our background includes robotics, simulation, and software development. We're looking for people interested in planetary science, geospatial data, engineering, and creative visualization.
summary:
LUNA VIEW is an interactive 3D lunar exploration and landing-site analysis platform developed by ZXC Team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by helping users understand how the Moon's terrain affects sunlight availability and geometric visibility of Earth.

Combining NASA LOLA elevation data, NASA PGDA high-resolution lunar terrain grids, and JPL Horizons astronomical observations, we developed a platform that transforms scientific datasets into an interactive lunar environment. Users can explore the Moon, examine three selected locations near the lunar South Pole, move observation points, visualize local terrain horizons, and identify time periods when both the Sun and Earth are geometrically visible.

Unlike a conventional 3D lunar map, LUNA VIEW connects terrain visualization with explainable scientific calculations, allowing users to understand not only whether visibility is possible, but also which surrounding terrain formations influence it.

Our goal is to make complex lunar environmental data more accessible and support better-informed decisions for future lunar exploration and mission planning.
details:
LUNA VIEW is an interactive 3D lunar exploration and landing-site analysis platform designed to help users understand how the Moon's terrain influences sunlight availability and geometric communication visibility with Earth.

The platform combines NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data and high-resolution lunar terrain grids with astronomical observations from the JPL Horizons System. Using these datasets, our software constructs local terrain horizons and compares them with the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth. Users can explore the lunar globe, examine three selected locations near the lunar South Pole, move observation points within supported areas, visualize surrounding terrain, and identify hourly samples when both the Sun and Earth are geometrically visible.

We developed an interactive 3D environment using JavaScript and Three.js, supported by HTML and CSS. The platform uses precomputed scientific datasets and calculations, allowing it to operate as a static web application without requiring a live server or external API requests.

Our creative approach combines scientific calculations with an accessible visual interface. Instead of simply displaying lunar maps, LUNA VIEW explains how nearby ridges, crater rims, and elevation differences affect visibility. We also considered terrain-data uncertainty, observation height, geographical coverage, and the limitations of hourly sampling.

The intended impact is to make complex lunar environmental data easier to explore and understand, supporting preliminary research and better-informed decisions in future lunar mission planning. LUNA VIEW is an exploratory analysis tool, not a landing-safety certification or a complete communication-link simulator.
